chunks.text: Privacy Commissioner coming in. Okay. Online. Yeah. Right. Right. So look, you're welcome to come to the table now. Thank you. So then we'll hear from our petitioner. Make it easier when we're replying. Right. Do we have Mr. Feldmann? Ms. Oh, sorry. Ms. Feldmann. So my apologies.

Yes, I'm here. Yes. Right, so I'm Greg O'Connor, the chair of the committee. We'll just get ourselves to introduce ourselves. To my right, my- I'm, so I'm Greg Fleming, the deputy chair of the committee. I'm Andrew Bailey. Kia ora, I'm Cindy Wade-Brown, Green List MP. All right. So thank you. Now you can take your submission as read.

We have 10 minutes. Obviously, feel free to speak to it, your points, but it would be good if you could leave time for questions. We also have the officials from the Ministry of Justice at the table. We'll be going to them afterwards for their oversight. So welcome.

That's great. Thank you. Thank you for having the opportunity to speak today. As you know, my name is Katja Feldmann. I'm a cybersecurity, governance, risk, and assurance professional with over 13 years of experience working across public and private sector organizations in New Zealand and internationally.

The reason I launched this petition is simple. As New Zealanders, we increasingly trust organizations with our most sensitive information, yet the consequences for failing to protect that information are often limited. My petition is not about punishing organizations that experience genuine cyber attacks, even if they take reasonable precautions. It's more about ensuring that there are adequate consequences where organizations fail to take reasonable steps to protect personal information or repeatedly neglect their

privacy obligations. All right. So that's sums up- Yeah... nice summary. And nothing else from -- Okay. Questions, members, then? I've taken the submission as read. I'm keen to get into the conversation with you. What's the, yeah- Yeah. Well, what we can do, so- I did have a question.

Thank you, Katja. You've listed the different penalties in different countries and showing that we're quite minimal. Have you seen evidence that those, which sort of penalty at what sort of level actually makes the difference in prevention? Because it's prevention we want, not so much the slapping of the wrist afterwards.

That's right. Unfortunately, I guess once the penalties are apply, you know, like if you were doing well in prevention, then you wouldn't get the penalty in the first place. There is a website which, I think it's called GDPR Tracker, that shows the different penalties for different organizations, including private and public sector. Sometimes you see a school, and then they get a very small penalty because they're a school, they're obviously teachers and educational professionals, so- Wow... it's quite a different approach. So I think the smaller penalties

are probably good for encouraging prevention and then the larger penalties when repeatedly, and this is what we have seen, I think, with the Privacy Commissioner, is where there repeatedly there are complaints, yet not much is done to actually prevent further damages there. Thank you.

Can I just, through you, Chair? Yeah. Mr. Bailey. Can I just ask a few questions? I was the minister for stopping scams, so I sort of had quite an interest in this. So there's two sides to the coin, and I wanted to understand your fundamental proposition before we jumped into the penalties. But so of course, there's two sides.

One is we have a lot of personal scams that occur because people are not good with passwords or all that type of scams, right? Yeah. The other thing is what we did and what I started was we're putting in place arrangements between the banks, then the telcos, and then there has been agreement with the Meta and the main digital providers.

Although that's probably more work to go in that field. So you're talking about scams, but I presume you're not talking about the personal, you're talking about the large-scale transfer of information, but it's occurred under an illegal process, and you'll know where most of these scams originate from as much as I do.

So are you dealing with those industrial leakages like we've had the, are you talking about the Hamilton Waikato University? How do you differentiate between all the other scams? We lose billions of dollars a year from personal scams. Sometimes, misinformation gets leaked but doesn't actually result in financial harm, might result in emotional harm. So what I'm trying to understand for you is what your proposition is.

I think essentially my proposition is probably having a look at the Privacy Act as a whole and seeing how it ties back to other legislation. Thinking like, if you look at the Health and Safety Act, for example, before that was tied to personal liability of directors of companies. It also was not always taken as seriously because- There's sort of two layers to it. So if you look at, I don't know if you've read recently, Booking.com had a big data breach, right?

So everyone that uses Booking.com, which is almost there's a lot of New Zealanders, no doubt, that use it. Booking.com failed to adequately protect the information of their users, and then they get a scam. So as the end user, like me opening that email, the more organizations fail to protect that information, and it leaks out to more different parties.

You just spread the attacks. We call it-... sort of the attack surface. It just spreads. So we're never going to get on top of scam if we keep leaking more and more- Yeah... of the information. Okay, now I agree with sort of what you're trying to do. But, so what you've said, just by inference from what you just said, is you don't want to deal with personal scams, where someone unwittingly does something, right? You're talking about gross misuse, transfer of data. Okay. So then there's sort of components within that, because you'll be

aware through your own work that there's certain organizations that get a high level of protection in New Zealand and are still subject to massive attacks where big data breaches. The hospital is one area of that. You'll probably know what I'm talking about.

Yep. And then large corporates, once you get below, I don't want to name companies, but are not inside that boundary. So are you talking about corporates here? Because your example was a corporate. Or you're talking about government agencies?

Both. But obviously for government agents. So it's not just about the penalties. I think it's, as government agencies, they already have a security sort of standard, which is the New Zealand Information- They still get, they still-... Security Manual. But they still lose information. Yeah, that's right. So I'm not sure if penalties would be the way to go because in the end they, I guess, are just taxpayer money.

But so there maybe needs to be some independent audits or something in that space. But in the private sector, I think penalties combined with some sort of legal obligation to actually do the... Because we're talking about prevention, right?

Ideally, we don't want anyone to pay that penalty. Yeah. Mm. So there's two areas. Then you sort of get that down to two areas. So one is what you, I think what you're saying there is there'd be a general, sort of a bit like a Companies Act requirement, a general requirement that if you possess people's personal details, then you need to show reasonable efforts to make sure that's protected.

That's fine. If you're subject to a concerted attack by one of the major players, and there's about four of them. Even small firms, I had a merchant bank, I lost some data at one stage. We had good systems, right? We took all the precautions, but we still lost data. And then the next point- Well, just on that one. Under that, that's a good example. So would, because they lost data, in Mr. Bailey's example, would that be almost a vicarious liability offense or a liability offense because they lost it?

I think if that, talk if that- Who would determine whether the degree of care exercised by Mr. Bailey's firm was adequate? And that's I guess, another layer of this, because we have the Privacy Act, but it's not very descriptive, right? So somewhere there needs to be some standards that say, "These are the minimum standards we expect organizations to follow."

And then if someone loses information, similar to what happened at Manage My Health now, you can go in there and you can say, "Well, legally you were supposed to follow this standard. Here's all the stuff you did, here's all the stuff you didn't do." And then- Okay. Now, Mr. Bailey, I think this is a good time actually to bring the officials in- Yeah. Can I just-... who've heard this. Okay, one last question.

But we can come back to, Ms. Sheldon. Just I think there's another angle which I think you were getting at as well, and this is what we tried to do with the banks and the telcos, and ultimately the measure of stuff is the sharing of knowledge. So if you have been attacked, the agreement that there is with the banks, for instance, is that they have to share that data, and they can share data simultaneously without being legally liable. So it's almost making sure that there is a network there that means that they can be protected,

and more readily therefore, more readily the key actors in the market, because most scams come through those three sources, are then stopped in their tracks much earlier than otherwise. So sharing data to stop the- Yeah... to, kind of- And that's a crucial bit- Or, well, look- A crucial part of it... okay, look, well, this, you've heard this, why it's useful to have you here. I'll just now invite our Ministry of Justice officials to take us away.

Kia ora koutou. Thank you for inviting us to speak with the committee. So the Ministry of Justice provided a written submission on the petition in April of this year, and in summary, that submission provided an overview of the current enforcement settings in the Privacy Act and the powers available to the Privacy Commissioner.

It noted the concerns of the petitioner's submission with the current enforcement and penalty settings in the Act, and also mentioned that we are developing advice on options to incentivize the protection of personal information as part of- The National Cybersecurity Action Plan 2026 to 2027.

So if there are no specific questions on what we provided in our written submission, I can just talk through the points we made in that submission. Do you want to- Or do you... No, you can... No, no. You should talk to- Yeah, no. So carry on All right. So, in terms of the Privacy Act, it came into effect on 1 December 2020. Its purpose is to protect and promote people's right to privacy over their personal information.

It applies to individuals and agencies. And when we say agencies, we mean agencies that decide to collect personal information for a particular purpose. And the Privacy Commissioner is an independent Crown entity, and he has a range of powers under the act, including resolving complaints and enforcing compliance.

The act is principles based rather than rules based. And the principles are intended to be flexible and proportionate, both to the range of agencies or organizations the act applies to, and based on the nature of the information they hold. So the act is quite context specific.

In terms of the commissioner's role, the commissioner has a role in terms of resolving individual complaints. So any person can make a complaint alleging that an action of an agency is an interference with their privacy, and then the commissioner will decide whether or not to investigate that complaint. And the complaint may lead to a settlement between the complainant and the agency, an assurance from the agency that the action will not be repeated.

The commissioner could investigate the complaint. The commissioner can make a referral to the Director of Human Rights, Review Tribunal proceedings. And the tribunal, the Human Rights Review Tribunal, may award remedies to an individual if satisfied that there has been a privacy interference, including damages up to a maximum of $350,000.

Then there are enforcement powers available to the commissioner. So I've just talked about the individual complaints that they deal with. But in terms of the enforcement powers of the commissioner, they can inquire into any matter that appears to be an infringement with the privacy of individuals, can investigate a complaint or a matter about which a complaint may be made under the act. They can issue compliance notices to agencies if they consider the agency has breached the act, a privacy principle, or a relevant code of practice.

And the compliance notice can sets out the nature of the breach, and then it can direct agencies to take specific steps to remedy the breach. And compliance notices are enforceable through the Human Rights Review Tribunal. And failure to comply with the tribunal is an offense. It's a criminal offense punishable by a fine of up to $10,000.

And then there are various other criminal offenses under the act, also punishable by a fine of up to $10,000 on conviction. In terms of the effectiveness of existing penalties and enforcement tools, the petitioner is correct to say that New Zealand is becoming somewhat of an outlier compared to privacy and regulatory settings internationally. Other jurisdictions certainly have strengthened regulatory powers in recent years.

So Australia, the EU, and the UK, they have introduced civil penalties for breaches of their privacy legislation, and the fines are in the millions. Australia, I think, most recently has gone up to 40 million. Mm-hmm. New Zealand's privacy law does not have civil penalties. And this is really because the act is based on an individual complaints model, and it's ensuring the commissioner can resolve complaints rather than enforce compliance.

So the recommendations in the petition that the act introduce a stronger penalty regime, for serious or repeated privacy breaches, are similar to what the privacy commissioner has called for in the past. Mm-hmm. In terms of our current work, we're working on advice on options to incentivize the protection of personal information, which could look at introducing penalties into the Privacy Act.

So- Are there any questions? Sorry. So it's work you're doing- Yes... under the auspices of the- The Cybersecurity Action Plan. Right. Okay. And will some of these recommendations... I mean, what are the terms of reference essentially for that?

Is it pretty wide-ranging to actually re- In terms of the recommendation? It's to- Or the terms of reference-... provide advice on options to incentivize the protection of personal information, including, for example, introducing civil penalties.

Right. When will you provide that advice? When? Yeah. Soon. Yes. And when do you reckon the cyber plan's going to be introduced? Well, the minister will make decisions, the Minister of Justice, in due course. Right. So imminent. So- It's subject to, yeah, the minister- Then your advice is imminent going to the Minister of Justice.

Shortly. Shortly. Very good. So let's just say these... Okay, so who's got the investigative team? Who has the ability to investigate these breaches? The Privacy Commissioner. They currently have the ability to investigate. Okay. And does he have the ability, or she, do they have the ability to do this? What sort of Because this is we- To investigate?

One, no. I think the Privacy Commissioner's clearly got the ability to investigate. Yeah. I think the question is does he have the capability? And secondly, my second question would be, has he undertaken any investigations in recent times? So is that a latent power or is it a power that's used actively?

Well, he most recently inquired into the Manage My Health data breach. Did anyone get fined, killed, taken to jail, locked up? Well, there were findings made in relation to that. So he found that both Manage My Health and Health New Zealand failed in their responsibilities to- But they opened the door, didn't they?

That's correct, and both breached rule five of- And did they get a penalty though? Well, no, because the commissioner does not have the ability to- How do you, and this is what the petitioner started asking, if you were to put a stronger regime in, who would prosecute in the case of the Waikato Hospital we talked about? Who would take it, and who would be sued? Is it the board?

Is it the managing director, or is it the CTO? And who would take that case? Who would take the case? Yeah, to sue them. One of the options is that the case would be taken by the commissioner-... but in the end it would be a court, the High Court- Yeah, but have you got funding for it?

... potentially that would decide. Have you got funding for it? Someone's got to put this, this to top my question, someone's got to put this. These are going to be massive cases, particularly against some of these big corporates. And it's hard to think that a couple of ex-cops working for the have got that capability to do it. And particularly once these fines get up around, if the recommendations that the sanctions become much greater.

But it would be done under the auspices of the Privacy Commissioner. Correct. Okay. I think we might have a talk afterwards about that. Yeah. There's the Privacy Commissioner now. Good. Well, actually, let's bring the Privacy Commissioner on right now. Good timing. Because we didn't know you were there. He was hidden. Secret agents.

Thank you. Afternoon, Mr. Chair, members. Good. Well, you've sat there, you've managed to hear the petitioner and ministry, so you can join all the bits up for us. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and I'm joined today by Ed Kennedy and Ushana Jayasuriya from my office, from the policy team.

Very briefly, as the submitter has noted, and as you will be aware, my office continues to see serious privacy breaches happening. As has just been referred to, most recently, the Manage My Health inquiry. We have formally reported on phase one of the inquiry, and our finding that they had breached what is known as Rule 5 of the Health Information Privacy Code has led to us saying publicly that we will issue compliance notices to them. Which is a tool available in our regulatory toolbox to direct them to take certain action or to stop doing certain

things to ensure that they come back within their operations within the ambit of the requirements of the Privacy Act. That, at the moment, is the most significant tool in many ways in our regulatory toolbox. Given that this is a petition, Mr. Chair, I thought members might be interested to know a little bit about what we're hearing from members of the public.

We've just conducted our 2026 privacy survey, which shows that concerns about privacy in general are deepening and diversifying. Not only are more people concerned about their individual privacy than ever before, but a greater number are saying that in the last few years they've become more and more concerned, which I think is a reflection of the significant cyber attacks and data privacy breaches we've seen over recent years.

Our survey actually asked questions around the matter that is part of the topic of the petition today, and New Zealanders continue to support the need for greater enforcement powers under the Act, with support from over 70% of the respondents. Of those, 75% of those respondents wanted to see higher penalties, and 74% supported audit powers, something else referred to by the petitioner. So there is a strong degree of public interest and support for what I would describe as adding another tool to the regulatory toolbox of this office. A financial penalty regime

is one tool in the compliance enforcement toolbox. It's an important tool, and it's a missing tool. We do actually regulate along a spectrum. For agencies that are trying to do privacy well, we might encourage, educate, provide guidance, provide warnings, those sorts of ends of the regulatory spectrum.

But at the other end, Mr. Chair, members, where we see poor or deliberate mismanagement of people's personal information, we believe that's where we need to have a stronger set of tools available to us. We have the compliance notice approach, as I've outlined, but also the ability, like my colleagues in other countries, to seek financial penalties through the court system or indeed to even issue infringement fines for lower level breaches of privacy is something that we believe is something that is needed in our operations.

I guess in many ways, though, our focus is also on building what I'd describe as the privacy fence at the top of the cliff, rather than always being the privacy ambulance at the bottom dealing with- These extraordinary large data privacy breaches and complaints from individuals about interference with their privacy.

So as part of a legislative reform package, we would also, and have in the past, advocated for things like audit powers for the office, for agencies like public and private sector organizations to be subject to accountability principles that require them to be more transparent, I guess, about what they're doing to ensure that they both protect and respect individuals' personal information.

But as the committee will know and has heard, the office of the Ministry of Justice is responsible for privacy policy. We're very much the regulator in this space. It is up to the Ministry and the government of the day to decide whether they wish to advance reform along these lines. We're very supportive of the direction of reform in terms of a financial penalty power for this office.

We would exercise that carefully. I can talk, if the committee wishes, about the sort of thing we might be talking about, and perhaps in comparison terms that some members will be familiar with, if you're interested, Mr. Chair. For example, if you think about the Commerce Commission in relation to the Fair Trading Act, they have a similar financial penalty regime.

So probably looking at a financial penalty regime consistent with consumer law, that sort of thing. Officials, of course, have a better understanding of the nature of the different financial penalty regimes that apply across different regulatory areas. But we're not looking for something extraordinary.

We're looking for something that would allow us to send a strong signal for the most egregious and poor management of people's personal information. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you. Just a question. Say, the Waikato Hospital breach. There's presumably an inquiry into the breaches, into the hackers.

That's done currently by police. Yeah. So there's that inquiry as to the criminals who have gone in and stolen the information. That's- And number- That's separate to any inquiry regarding the privacy issue, presumably. Is that it? That's right. If criminal action activity has taken place, for example, hackers are breaking into, the most recent case, ManageMyHealth, that is something for the police to consider looking at. But under our current privacy law, if you suffer what is defined as a serious privacy breach, you have to, by law, report that to my office, and we have the ability to assess

that and, if we wish, to investigate that to see what happened and why, and whether appropriate and reasonable steps were taken in terms of the requirements you need to meet to protect personal information in Privacy Act, to see whether those requirements were in fact actually met. So do you work -- well, presumably there is a criminal inquiry into ManageMyHealth.

So will you be working with the police on that? I'm not sure if there is actually going on at the moment in that area. We have completed our report into phase one, which found that both ManageMyHealth and Health New Zealand failed to have in place reasonable security safeguards to protect individuals' personal information.

So from my perspective, they failed to meet the requirements of the Privacy Act, which is why we're taking further regulatory action in response to that. The actual identification of the hackers is not something that we would necessarily be interested in, and that would be a matter for police. But we understand that actually identifying who those hackers might be and then holding them to account is in itself a very challenging thing to do.

Well, you'd need to find out how they got in, though, wouldn't you? Because that's going to be very much part of if you're going to take a case against ManageMyHealth, then part of the actus reus is going to be finding out how the people got in. So I'm just surprised you wouldn't be working more closely with them.

Well, as part of our inquiry, Mr. Chair, we actually brought in specialist forensic IT support to assist my team here, and they were able to help us identify the failures in security from the agency concerned and to identify what hardening and strengthening of systems now needs to happen. So we brought that in ourselves.

As Eva said, I think we know it was the hacker group Kazoo, I think they were called. These are often based in countries a long way away from here, Mr. O'Connor, and kind of difficult and beyond the reach of our authorities. But the privacy failure, if proved, is something that we very much can and do have a say and have a look at.

We want to make sure they're not in Te Awamutu though, don't we? Mr. Bailey. Yeah. Can I just ask a couple questions? One is jurisdiction. You can require any entity, whether private or government entity, that every entity is subject to Privacy Act?

That's right. It's an extraordinarily broad remit, so all public and private sector entities from the large corporate to the corner store, non-governmental organizations, all those sorts of groups. Okay. And in terms of actions, have you taken anyone to court? Not in my time as Privacy Commissioner, and I don't think so before then, no.

I don't believe we've ever prosecuted anyone. But that begs the question- Mm... even if you increase the penalties- Mm... why haven't you? And I presume one of a significant issue in terms of funding of your office, capability, expense of taking court cases to the High Court. Can you say why you haven't taken any cases?

Sure. We've operated to date on the basis of the current tools available to us, and the most commonly used and powerful one for us is the compliance notice. So we don't need to go down the court route. Prosecutions under our act are normally in relation to a failure to follow, for example, the requirements of a compliance notice. So it's failure to follow lawfully the requirements imposed on an agency by this office.

If we- So you basically have to go through a two-step. Yeah. One is to issue the notice. If they don't do anything, then you have to... But what happens if there's gross negligence? Yeah. Because it's different cases, and I don't know whether you heard me talking before, but we've got an orchestrated actor, and there's many well-known actors are doing it.

And that's a national level. Even if you have a very good system, then a lot of people will be subject. Even the American major institutions have been hacked. So there's an issue of graduation- Yeah... but then there's a system of where there's a gross, let's say Hamilton, on the primary facie, where it was a gross case of doing silly stuff, right? Negligence.

Presumably, you'd also want the power to be able to take them straight to court for an appropriate, rather than just go through this graduated process. Or is that not your preference? Yes. Absolutely. So what I was saying was if we had a financial penalty regime specified in the Privacy Act, what we would do would be, having assessed the nature of a breach, the reasons for it, if it was due to deliberate or incredibly poor management by the agency's governance and leadership concerned, we may well decide to go down the financial

penalty regime and seek a financial penalty through the court system. And you're absolutely right, Mr. Bayly. We would then need to have the ability to fund such court action. Yes. So really what we're hearing is Ms. Feldman is right, that there is, currently, we really are without a regime that's going to give meaningful sanction and to organizations which don't adequately protect the information they have, the personal information they have. Would that be fair from your point of view?

Absolutely, Mr. Chair. A financial penalty regime immediately sharpens that sense of accountability around the boardroom table. It provides a demonstration effect to other actors in that area as well. If they can see one of their colleagues in whatever sector of activity that's going on, let's say it's the health sector or the banking sector.

If they see someone being hit with a large fine, it'll make everybody sit up and pay attention. It makes the board of directors turn to the chief executive and say, "What kind of work are you doing to harden, for example, your IT systems?" So it has a positive effect beyond the agency concerned. So presumably, this conversation has taken place elsewhere, that Ms. Feldman's not the only person who's been concerned about this.

No, I have been talking about it since I took up this role four years ago. I've been speaking to my colleagues in other countries about what they're doing in this space. We're seeing a greater degree of using this tool coming through from our Australian colleagues, for example. And as you've heard from the Ministry of Justice, this is something that they're looking at as well and has indeed been put forward as something that needs some serious thought as part of the government of the day's cybersecurity action plan, as you've heard.

Well, I'd say that we're yet as a committee to meet and discuss that, but it may well be that that will be our own conclusion from what we've heard today. Members, are there any other questions- There was one other dimension... of any of our officials or in fact even our petitioner? Commissioner, I don't know whether you heard before, but the other element is you talked about prevention, and there is a prevention.

If there is a breach, let's say of number of organizations. As the minister put that thing in place with the banks, it's now been rolled out with telecom and the other internet providers. But one of the key components of that was to be able to share when they were aware of attacks, particularly in the relation to scams.

The way you framed it, if someone has got a breach of data, they've got to send it to you. First of all, do you share that data immediately with the relevant people to say, "We're aware of this"? Or you don't get that in real time, so by the time you get it, it's too late? Or do you allow those organizations make other people aware of what's happening, and there's a mechanism to do that really quickly? Because that's in the best interests of New Zealand, not just an organization.

Sure. A couple of things on that, and I'll ask my colleague to talk as well. Breach reporting to us is treated with a high degree of confidentiality, because the fact that there has been a breach for a particular organization may actually be even market sensitive, and so they need to be careful about how they message that and plan for that. Second, in my time in the role, I've had a number of meetings, for example, with the banking ombudsman, with the Bankers Association, with banks to discuss that very issue, to ensure that they have

the freedom to share information in a way that, while respecting people's privacy, allows the goal of protecting individuals' financial stewardship to be protected as well. Eve, anything further? Yeah. On that point, my team has been involved in the Anti-Scam Alliance work, so the collaboration pillar for the Anti-Scam Alliance about information sharing to- prevent and detect scams. The other point I'd note is just that the commissioner has powers under the act to refer matters on to other agencies where appropriate, if it's

an issue that's better placed resolved by another regulatory agency, for example. So we have information sharing powers to give effect to that under our act already as well. And one other question. If an organization is hacked, and the blackmail, what's the word, that they're blackmailed to- Yeah... give the information back, and they do that, and they don't report to their customers that that information was hacked.

Do you deal with that? Is it an offense to do that? Yeah. It's a breach of the Privacy Act to not report a, what we would regard as a serious breach. And so what we do see, Mr. Chair, is organizations reporting breaches to us that might not be serious because people from abundance of caution are now getting into the habit of doing that.

The sorts of organizations that would be reluctant to report a breach are the sorts of organizations that we would have the greatest degree of concern about, and probably would be looking at to hit with a financial penalty if we found that they had been poor stewards of the personal information that they had available to them. Absolutely.

All right. And just finally, so we're going to have to keep moving, but- Yeah... we've had the justice officials, we've had a very well-informed petitioner, and yourselves. The Petitions Committee will be looking to report on this. Is there anyone else that you would suggest we should be talking to or hearing from here that would be able to enlighten us a little further about this from the top of your head? Or even if you were to afterwards think of anyone, we'd be quite here because we see this as a search for an answer, and making sure we have all the facts available.

So if any other petitioners actually, or any of our submitters, thought there was anyone else, any industry bodies that might be worth talking to? Certainly. Even a quick Google search of financial penalties privacy will throw up a number of both NGO expert privacy consultancy law firm commentators talking about the value of a financial penalty regime in this space.

As I said, as part of a regulatory toolkit. One tool, an important tool, but remembering that there are others as well. All right. Any other pressing questions, members? All right. And back to our petitioner. Thank you very much. I would like to think what we exist for, to make sure that someone like yourself with that knowledge can bring it forward, and hopefully we can report and either, if not get things moving, lubricate the wheels.
Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you... things are already happening. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Bye.
